summary: Australian reviewers consistently rate the Sealion 6 as the value pick of the plug-in hybrid SUV class, with the Essential holding the title of the country's cheapest new PHEV and offering a genuinely usable electric-only range. Opinions are more mixed on dynamics: reviewers like the improved, comfort-biased suspension tune but mark it down for body roll and light, indirect steering next to rivals such as the Cupra Formentor. Most agree the 425-litre boot is a real compromise versus segment rivals, and that running costs climb sharply once the battery is depleted.
pros: Essential undercuts the Toyota RAV4 PHEV and Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV by a wide margin at $42,990 before on-roads, reviewers' benchmark for value in the class
Usable electric-only range for a budget PHEV: up to 92km (Essential) or 140km (Dynamic Extended Range) on a full charge, enough to cover most Melbourne commutes without touching the engine
Generous standard equipment for the price, including a rotating touchscreen (12.8in Essential/Dynamic, 15.8in Premium), dual-zone climate and vehicle-to-load power
Five-star ANCAP rating (assessed under 2023 Euro NCAP criteria) with seven airbags standard across the range
8-year/160,000km battery warranty outlasts the vehicle's own 6-year/150,000km unconditional term
cons: 425-litre boot with the rear seats up trails segment rivals like the Toyota RAV4 and Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV, the direct cost of packaging the battery under the floor

Once the battery is depleted the Sealion 6 drinks far more than its 0.8-1.1L/100km label figure suggests — reviewers measured 4.8-6.0L/100km in charge-sustaining running — so the economics case weakens sharply for anyone who cannot charge at home
Soft, comfort-tuned suspension brings noticeable body roll and light, indirect steering that reviewers rate well behind more dynamically composed rivals
No spare wheel, a tyre-repair kit only, and BYD's Australian resale value and dealer/service network remain relatively unproven for a car this new to the range
